title: A Hymn for the House
premise: Jude Nystrom hosts the graveyard-shift call-in show 'Static Hymns' from a rented house on Vesper Lane, and one night the callers are all people who died the week before — including the previous tenant, whose death Jude unknowingly inherited along with the lease. As mirrors begin lagging a single second behind reality, Jude realizes the house itself is a receiver, and something has been using their show as an invitation, gathering a congregation of the dead in the walls. The truth surfaces: the house's original owner conducted séances to keep her dead daughter 'on air,' and the ritual requires a living broadcaster willing to listen. In the final hours before sunrise, Jude must choose between cutting the signal forever — erasing the found family of voices that made them feel seen — or letting the house take them as its new permanent host, a choice they resolve by broadcasting the truth aloud, breaking the invitation's consent clause and freeing the dead at the cost of the show, the house, and nearly themselves.
about_author: Ulyana Whitlock is a former overnight radio producer who spent six years answering phones for insomniacs, conspiracy theorists, and the grieving, and claims every ghost story she writes began as a caller who never hung up. She lives in a drafty farmhouse with a wall of dead radios she refuses to repair.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. We meet Jude mid-broadcast, a ritual of documentation — logging every call, every voice — and learn they moved to Vesper Lane to disappear after a public breakdown. The last caller of the night says, 'You're in my house now,' and hangs up. Beat: lonely competence cracking into unease.

chapters.title: The Previous Tenant
chapters.summary: Jude researches the caller's name and finds an obituary: the man died eight days before Jude signed the lease. POV shifts to a log-entry structure, Jude transcribing the call. Emotional beat: the first crack in their belief that documentation keeps them safe.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The bathroom mirror shows the room a heartbeat behind — Jude raises a hand, the reflection follows late. They test every mirror, film them, timestamp the footage. Beat: clinical dread; Jude's coping mechanism (measuring, recording) becomes a horror instrument.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: On air, the dead call in: a drowned girl, a retired teacher, all dead within the same week, all asking Jude to 'keep the line open.' Jude's POV interleaved with call transcripts. Beat: terrible tenderness — Jude, starved for connection, starts to care about the voices.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Know
chapters.summary: Jude befriends Marisol, a night-shift nurse next door, the first living human contact in months. Marisol mentions the house's reputation: people who live there 'stop being seen.' Beat: warmth and warning entwined; found family's first thread.

chapters.title: The House Remembers
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. They find the previous tenant's hidden recordings in the crawlspace — his own mirror-lag documentation, ending mid-sentence. The lag is now two seconds. Beat: Jude realizes they are following a script already performed, a role the house has cast before.

chapters.title: Congregation
chapters.summary: The dead appear at the windows at 3 a.m., not threatening — waiting, hymnals of static in their hands. Jude's POV, half-awake. Beat: awe curdling into the understanding that they are not haunted; they are hosting.

chapters.title: Marisol Sees It Too
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She witnesses the lag in her own phone's front camera and comes to Jude, breaking her own isolation. Beat: alliance formed; two lonely people choosing each other despite the danger.

chapters.title: The Séance Broadcasts
chapters.summary: Jude finds the original owner's diaries: Edith Vesper, 1930s radio pioneer, who held séances over her own transmitter to keep her dead daughter broadcasting. Beat: revelation of the house's purpose — it was built as an antenna for grief.

chapters.title: The Invitation Clause
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, decoding Edith's notes: the ritual requires a living voice that consents to listen, night after night. Every broadcast was a signature. Jude has been inviting them in. Beat: guilt and horror — their one comfort was the trap.

chapters.title: Static Hymns, Final Season
chapters.summary: Jude tries to quit the show; the station replaces them, but the replacement host quits after one night, weeping. The dead only answer to Jude. Beat: the trap of being needed; power over the dead revealed as the house's corruption of empathy.

chapters.title: The Lag Spreads
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The delay reaches three seconds; reflections begin acting independently — showing the room as it will be, not as it is, and in one reflection Marisol sees Jude's chair empty. Beat: foreshadowing loss; the found family faces its first fracture.

chapters.title: Edith's Daughter
chapters.summary: A new caller: a small voice claiming to be Edith's daughter, still broadcasting from 1938, asking Jude to 'let Mama sleep.' Jude's POV. Beat: pity weaponized — the house uses the most sympathetic ghost to secure consent.

chapters.title: Do Not Answer After Sunrise
chapters.summary: Jude and Marisol fortify the house: covering mirrors, unplugging radios, agreeing on rules. The dead grow insistent, then angry, then hurt. Beat: siege preparation; the horror of hurting ghosts who only want to be heard.

chapters.title: The Voice in Jude's Mouth
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. During a forced broadcast, the house speaks through them, promising the congregation that Jude will 'stay on air forever.' They come to, lips raw, three hours missing from their log. Beat: loss of bodily autonomy; documentation fails them for the first time.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She tries to take Jude's place as listener, offering her own consent, and the house considers it — the mirrors show Marisol's reflection staying behind when she turns away. Beat: sacrifice offered; found family tested at its deepest level.

chapters.title: The Truth About the Daughter
chapters.summary: Jude finds Edith's final tape: her daughter never died — Edith kept her alive past death by feeding the house listeners, and the girl has been begging for release for ninety years. Beat: the central lie exposed; grief itself was the corruption.

chapters.title: Nightfall on Vesper Lane
chapters.summary: The longest night. The dead fill the house, the mirrors show only the congregation, and the walls hum with a hymn in static. Jude and Marisol, back to back, prepare the final broadcast. Beat: calm before climax; resolve crystallizing.

chapters.title: On Air
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. They take the microphone one last time and broadcast the truth — Edith's crime, the invitation's mechanics, the daughter's imprisonment — knowing that informed listeners cannot be 'invited,' only witnesses. The house screams through the speakers. Beat: climax; truth as exorcism.

chapters.title: The Daughter's Silence
chapters.summary: The girl's voice, freed, sings one clear note and the congregation follows — a hymn that unbuilds the house's frequency. Marisol's POV as mirrors shatter in sequence, each releasing a lagging second of stored time. Beat: catharsis; the dead choosing to let go.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Dawn. The house is just a house — but it demands payment: Jude's voice is gone, hoarse to a whisper, their show and their invisibility traded away. Marisol stays. Beat: bittersweet cost; Jude can no longer hide, and no longer wants to.

chapters.title: A Hymn for the House
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Jude's POV. Months later, Jude and Marisol host a small living-listeners show from a new apartment; the final call of the first episode is static that almost, almost forms a thank-you. Jude logs it anyway. Documentation, they write, is still a kind of prayer. Beat: quiet resolution; memory kept without being owned by it.
